title: Gender and Negotiation
description: Women often face a 'likeability penalty' for negotiating assertively, which changes the dynamic—but not because women are less capable.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Women often face a 'likeability penalty' for negotiating assertively, which changes the dynamic—but not because women are less capable.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A woman who asks for a raise using direct, self-focused language may be rated as 'pushy.' The same words from a man are rated as 'confident.'
When women negotiate on behalf of a team or client ('My team has achieved X, so we're looking for Y'), the penalty often disappears.
Many women avoid negotiating entirely when the situation is ambiguous, losing thousands over a career.

sections.title: Common Phrases That Reduce Backlash
content: 'Based on my contributions to the team's results...' (ties request to collective benefit).
'I've been advised to ask for a market adjustment...' (references an external standard).
'I'd like to work together to find a solution that reflects my contribution to this company.'

sections.title: Protection Strategy (for Everyone)
content: Make the negotiation about value and fairness, not personality.
If you're a manager, explicitly state, 'I expect people to negotiate; it won't affect how I view them.' This removes the ambiguity that triggers the gap.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The gender gap in negotiation is not about ability; it's about the social cost of self-advocacy. Reframing reduces that cost.
